title_content.content: Promoting strength-ductility synergy by heterogeneous grain structure in a zirconium-alloyed Fe-Mn-Al-C low-density steel

paragraph_content.content: Yuheng Wang , Runze Yu , Fengchao An <sup>*</sup> , Suotao Wang <sup>**</sup>, Hao Wang , Zibo Zhao , Hongpu Yue , Tianxiang Gao , Junting Luo <sup>***</sup>, Junsong Zhang , Riping Liu
Center of Advanced Structured Materials, State Key Laboratory of Metastable Materials Science and Technology, Yanshan University, Qinhuangdao, 066004, China

title_content.content: A R T I C L E I N F O

paragraph_content.content: Keywords: Low-density steels Bimodal grains Zirconium addition Mechanical properties

title_content.content: A B S T R A C T

paragraph_content.content: Heterostructures, particularly dual-phase heterostructures, often lead to hetero-interfacial stress concentration, and ultimately premature failure. though they benefit from heterogeneous deformation. Addressing the challenge of strain localization and hetero-interfacial cracking, a single-phase heterogeneous grain structure is designed through tuning zirconium (Zr) content and employing precise thermo-mechanical treatment. As Zr content in creases to 0.50 wt %, a single-phase bimodal grain structure is successfully engineered, including soft coarse grain zones (~5 μm in size and 65 % in area) and hard fine grain zones (~1 μm in size and 35 % in area). Such bimodal heterostructure is mainly ascribed to the retarding effect of recrystallization, due to the drag effect of Zr atoms and Zener pinning of ZrC. The synergistic effects of microstructural heterogeneity and ZrC precipitation enhance the strengths. Furthermore, multistage deformation mechanisms, involving heterogeneous deformationinduced hardening, dislocation slip and nanotwinning, enable the strain hardening capability and ductility.

For structural alloys used in engineering applications, the simulta neous enhancement of strength and ductility remains a critical chal lenge. Recently, the Fe-Mn-Al-C-based steels have grained considerable attention, due to the desirable strength-ductility synergy and lightness [1–3]. To further enhance their mechanical properties, utilizing inco herent B2 intermetallic compounds has been a vital approach through addition of Ni [4,5]. However, such precipitation strengthening effect usually leads to a significant enhancement of strengths accompanied by a ductility loss, namely strength-ductility trade-off [6].

Recent development on alloys with heterostructues has a great po tential to breakthrough such trade-off, thereby leading to various het erostructures introduced by different approaches including muti-phase structures [7,8], gradient grains [9], multi-modal grain structures [7–9]. For these heterostructures, the extra strengthening and hardening de pends on the difference in hardness between the soft and hard regions, which is usually referred as heterogeneous deformation-induced (HDI) effect [7,8]. However, the pronounced disparity between soft and hard zones (e.g., hardness and elastic modulus) often induces the interfacial strain localization and premature failure, such as different dual-phase systems including FCC/B2 dual-phase steels [10], and FCC/L2 me dium entropy alloys [11,12]. In comparison to these dual-phase alloys, heterogeneous grain structures usually exhibit hardness difference and an identical elastic modulus between soft and hard zones [13,14], owing to the single-phase structure. Such microstructural heterogeneities can effective mitigate strain localization via reducing disparity between hard and soft zones. Thus, introducing a single-phase heterogeneous grain structure is a promising pathway to enhancing the strength and ductility.

Following this line of thought, we introduce heterostructure grain structure via a combination of thermo-mechanical treatment (TMT) and addition of Zr. A typical single-phase heterostructure grain structure including coarse grains and fine grains is successfully designed via tuning Zr content. Such heterostructure effectively provides an extra strengthening and hardening effect, thereby further enhancing the strength and strain hardening capability.

paragraph_content.content: Three Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steels were melted using a vacuum arc-melt furnace, and their chemical compositions are Fe-25Mn-7Al-0.9C-0Zr. Fe-25Mn-7Al-0.9C-0.01Zr and Fe-25Mn-7Al-0.9C-0.50Zr (wt. %), which are referred to as Zr0, Zr0.01 and Zr0.50 steels, respec tively. For the melting process, the raw materials (>99.8 wt % pure) were placed into the water-cooled copper crucible. Then, the furnace was evacuated to a high vacuum level (the pressure below

bar) to avoid gas contamination including oxygen (O), nitrogen (N) and hydrogen (H). Additionally, introducing high-purity argon (Ar) into the furnace chamber (a pressure below 1 bar) prevents the oxidation and contamination. Repeating melting was conducted at least five times to further promote the uniformly chemical compositions and reduce the gas contamination. Such melting process including high-purity raw materials, a high vacuum level and high-purity argon can effectively achieve the average content of O (12–89 ppm [15]), N (~18 ppm [16]) and H (~2 ppm [17])during the steelmaking process. These as-cast steels were subjected to homogenization (1200 <sup>◦</sup>C for 2 h), and Fig. S1 reveals that the oxygen segregate to grain boundaries does not occur. Then, hot-rolling with a thickness reduction of 40 %, followed by water quenching. These hot-rolled plates were subjected to cold rolling process with an 80 % reduction. Then, the Zr-alloyed cold-rolled plates were annealed at 900 <sup>◦</sup>C for 5 min, followed by water-quenching.

For the room temperature tensile experiments, flat dog-bone-shaped samples with a gauge length of 14 mm and width of 4 mm were prepared from the cold-rolling plate along rolling direction (RD). 3.1. Microstructures of the Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steels with different Zr content prior to deformation

Fig. 1 shows the microstructure of the Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steel with different Zr content prior to tensile deformation. As shown in Fig. 1a, the microstructure of the Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steel without Zr is mainly composed of coarse recrystallized FCC grains, indicating that the steel annealed at 900 <sup>◦</sup>C is subjected to full recrystallization. As adding Zr into the Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steel, Fig. 1b reveals that the microstructure of the Zr0.01 steel consists of coarse FCC grains and few fine FCC grains. With increasing Zr content to 0.50 wt %, the micro structure of the Zr0.50 steel exhibits a typical heterogeneous feature, i. e., coarse FCC grains (CG) and fine FCC grains (FG), as captured in Fig. 1c. An enlarged BSE image (Fig. 1c ) clearly reveals that a high density of fine FCC particles is uniformly distributed in the FG regions.

To further reveal the microstructure evolution of the Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steels, the EBSD analysis was conducted and the results are shown in Fig. 2. For the Zr0 steel, the EBSD data including inverse pole figure (IPF), image quality (IQ) and kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps (Fig. 2a–a<sub>2</sub>) reveal that its microstructure has equiaxed FCC grains with low KAM values. Further adding micro-alloyed Zr in the Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steel, the average size of recrystallized FCC grains is

paragraph_content.content: obviously reduced and their grain orientations are also random, as shown in Fig. 2b–b . Differently, Fig. 2c–c reveals that the micro structure exhibits a distinct heterostructure including CG zones and FG zones. Compared to the CG zones with low KAM values, the FG zones exhibit a high KAM value, indicating a high density of dislocations are decorated in these fine FCC grains.

According to the BSE images and EBSD data, more microstructural details of CG zones and FG zones, including their average sizes and area fraction, are estimated and shown in Fig. 3. As shown in Fig. 3a, the fraction of fine grains is significantly increased (0 % → 35 %), as increasing Zr content from 0 wt% to 0.50 wt %. For the average size of FCC grains (Fig. 3b–d), the average size of FCC grains is obviously reduced (12 μm → 7 μm) when the steel is added to 0.01 wt % Zr. Further adding Zr into the steel (i.e., Zr0.50 steel), the FCC grains exhibit a bimodal distribution of 5 μm and 1 μm, resulting from the heterogeneous structure including CG zones and FG zones, which stands in contrast to the homogeneous FCC grains in Zr0 steel and Zr0.01 steel. These results suggest that increasing Zr content can lead to a heterogeneous archi tecture of FCC matrix.

Fig. 4a shows the engineering stress-strain curves of the Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steels with different Zr content. In Zr0 steel, its yield strength is ~435 MPa, the ultimate tensile strength is 820 MPa, and fracture ductility is 52 %. As Zr content increased to 0.01 wt %, the strengths of the Zr0.01 steel are slightly increased, i.e., yield strength: ~450 MPa, ultimate tensile strength: ~832 MPa, while its fracture ductility is increased to 55 %. With further increasing of Zr content, the Zr0.50 steel exhibits a reasonable strength-ductility combination, i.e., yield strength: ~505 MPa, ultimate tensile strength: ~855 MPa and fracture ductility: 58 %. Similarly, a high true ultimate tensile strength and true strain is observed in the Zr0.50 steel. This suggests that intro ducing heterostructure in Fe-Mn-Al-C low-density steels through addi tion of Zr can enhance the mechanical properties. The microscopic fracture morphologies of these fractured Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steels are shown in Fig. 4b–d. For the Zr0 steel, its facture surface is mainly composed of small dimples and cleavage faces. As the Zr content increasing, the dimples are obviously larger and deeper than those in Zr0 steel. and the density is also increased.

To reveal the strain partitioning behavior in the hetero-structured Zr0.50 steel, the von Mises maps are obtained from quasi in-situ μ-DIC as a function of global strain in Fig. 5. The EBSD-IQ map (Fig. 5a) shows the measured area comprising the coarse FCC grains and fine FCC grains. As illustrated in Fig. 5b, significant strain partitioning is observed at a minor plastic strain of 2 %. The CG zones and hetero-interfaces between FG and CG zones experiences high strain, whereas the FG zones remain nearly undeformed. This is mainly attributed to the hardness differences between CG zones (soft regions) and FG zones (hard regions). As the global strain increased to 8 % (Fig. 5c), the local strain of the FG zones becomes more pronounced, indicating that the strain partitioning be tween soft and hard regions persists during plastic deformation. Such strain partitioning behavior leads to the generation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs), promoting a heterogeneous deformation-induced (HDI) strengthening [7,8].

paragraph_content.content: fracture surface, the severe deformed FCC matrix (Fig. 6b) exhibits a high density of slip bands along 111planes, which generally leads to a strengthening effect [18]. Excepted for dislocations, nanotwins with ~20 nm in size are generated during a heavy deformation. as evidenced by a TEM imaging (Fig. 6c). In the meantime, a high density of dislo cation is decorated around the nanotwinned region, which contributes to the interaction between dislocations and nanotwins. Such behavior further effectively reduces the mean free paths of mobile dislocations, thereby leading to a typical twinning-induced plasticity. Fig. 6c reveals that twin boundaries are decorated by multiple stacking faults, which indicates that the nanotwins formation originates from the transition from multiple Shockley partial dislocations to twins [19]. In addition to the deformation behaviors of FCC matrix, Fig. 6d shows that numerous particles with ~30 nm in size are distributed in FCC grain interior, which can effectively inhibit the movement of dislocations, i.e., pre cipitation strengthening. A detail analysis on these nanoscale particles via HRTEM and corresponding FFT pattern (Fig. 6d ) confirms that these nanosized particles are identified as ZrC carbides, due to the addition of Zr and the strong affinity between Zr and C [20].

title_content.content: 4.1. Formation mechanism of the heterogeneous grain structure

paragraph_content.content: In general, heterogeneous grain structures, e.g., bimodal recrystal lized grains (CG/FG zones) [9], recrystallized and non-recrystallized zones [13], are designed through introducing partial recrystallization. The TMT, i.e., severe cold-rolling and various annealing conditions, is a significant approach for the partial recrystallization. In present work, a typical TMT treatment including 80 % cold-rolling and short-time annealing
( 9 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }

for 5 min) was applied in the Fe-Mn-Al-C steels. However, the Zr0 steel exhibits a homogeneous grain structure after the TMT treatment. Interestingly, the combination of TMT treatment and Zr addition leads to a heterogeneous grain structure including CG and FG zones. As increasing Zr content, the fraction of FG zones is obviously increased (Fig. 3). Thus, it is necessary to reveal the formation mecha nism of heterogeneous grain structure in Zr0.50 steel.
It is well accepted that recrystallization is driven by the stored energy of cold-rolled deformation, i.e., the high density of dislocations and shear bands. Such driving force

For the annealed Zr0.50 steel, Zr elements are mainly distributed in FCC matrix, except for precipitation of ZrC. Based on Equation (1), Zr in solid solution and ZrC precipitation exhibit a retarding effect of recrystallization. Specifically, these Zr elements distributed in FCC matrix serve as solute atoms, which usually diffuses to the vicinity of defects including grain boundaries, shear bands and dislocations. During annealing process, the accumulation of these Zr atoms in turn impedes the movement of grain boundaries and recovery of shear bands and dislocations. Such drag effect from Zr atoms leads to a high energy barrier of recrystallization of cold-rolled microstructure during anneal ing [11,22], thereby inducing the partial recrystallization. Further, ac cording to the thermodynamic calculation (Fig. 7), the fraction of ZrC particles is ~0.6 % after annealing at 900 <sup>◦</sup>C. These nanoscale ZrC particles also inhibit the migration of grain boundaries during recrys tallization through a typical Zener pinning effect. The Zener pinning force is usually related to the average size of precipitates and fraction of precipitates [23]. Compared to the Zr0 and Zr0.01 steels, the fraction of ZrC carbides in Zr0.50 steel is highest. Based on Fig. 6d, the size of ZrC in the Zr0.50 steel is only 30 nm. As a result, these nanoscale ZrC carbide in the Zr0.50 steel can lead to a desirable Zener pinning force, thereby playing a pivotal role of the partial recrystallization. Additionally, the micro shear bands caused by the heavy cold-rolling deformation are the preferred sites for the nucleation of recrystallization

, which provides the enough driving force to formation of fine grains. As a result, the synergetic effects of drag effect of Zr atoms, Zener pinning of ZrC and TMT treatment promote the heterogeneous grain structure in the Zr0.50 steel.

title_content.content: 4.2. Effect of heterogeneous grain structure on enhancing strength ductility synergy

For the yield strength, the bimodal heterogeneous grain structure induces an extra strengthening contribution (i.e., HDI strengthening), apart from traditional strengthening mechanisms, e.g., solid-solution strength ening, grain boundary strengthening and precipitation strengthening. Except for the enhanced yield strength, the Zr0.50 steel exhibits a remarkable strain hardening capability and fracture ductility, as shown in Fig. 4a. For the heterogeneous grain structure, a high density of GNDs is generated during the elasto-plastic co-deformation, as evidenced in Fig. 5b. Such high strengthening ef fect promotes the formation of deformation twinning, thereby enabling the further strain hardening capability. Thus, the synergic effects of HDI hardening and deformation twins provide a reasonable strain hardening rate, which further improves the fracture ductility.

In present study, a single-phase heterogeneous grain structure, con taining coarse grains with ~5 μm in size and 65 % in area and fine grains with ~1 μm in size and 35 % in area, is successfully engineered in a Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steel. As the Zr content increases to 0.50 wt %, the drag effect of Zr atoms and Zener pinning of ZrC carbides is obvious enhanced, which can retard the recrystallization process. Such retarding recrystallization in turn assists the formation of bimodal grain structure. The heterogeneous grain structure has yielded desirable enhancement in strength-ductility synergy, in comparison to the Fe-Mn-Al-C steels without Zr addition or with 0.01 wt % Zr addition. The significant strengthening effect is mainly attributed to the grain boundary strengthening, HDI strengthening and precipitation strengthening. For the enhanced strain hardening capability and fracture ductility, the deformation mechanisms are dominated by cooperating slip bands, HDI hardening and deformation twins.
